proposed_edges.relationship: Historians answer the deconstructive turn she helped bring into Indian history: Eaton names her 1985 reading of Subaltern Studies as a hinge of a turn to “literary criticism” whose costs he finds greater than its gains (2000); Moran rereads the Sirmur records behind her 1985 archive essay and finds the rani “an astute ruler” (2014)
proposed_edges.map_label: Eaton and Moran: historians against the reading, 2000–14
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Two named historians without nodes, drawn from the entry for historians' responses to postmodernism (the pattern of edge_257 and edge_933). Richard M. Eaton, "(Re)imag(in)ing Other²ness: A Postmortem for the Postmodern in India" (Journal of World History 11:1, 2000), read pp. 57–61 and 77–78: the collective moved "from a positivist and empiricist orientation to one grounded more squarely in a literary criticism"; in Subaltern Studies IV (1985) "Gayatri Spivak criticized subalternist historians for having adopted positivist methodologies" and, "herself a literary critic, urged historians to continue their efforts to recover subaltern consciousness even while knowing this was impossible" (p. 60); the turn's "modest reminder" is "vastly outweighed" by "an ahistorical and structuralist methodology incapable of explaining historical particularity" (p. 78). His target is the postmodern turn in Indian history as a whole, with Spivak and Cohn as named hinges. Arik Moran, "'The Rani of Sirmur' Revisited" (Modern Asian Studies 49:2, 2015; online 17 September 2014), read in part: "a close reading of the records reveals profound discrepancies between Spivak's interpretation and conditions that existed in and around the kingdom at the time"; the rani "was actually an astute ruler"; her "misreading of evidence goes beyond the boundaries of the discipline as such", although "her fresh approach to source material does point to the cardinal importance of interdisciplinary research". Moran cites Eaton (n. 3). Her 1985 History and Theory essay is unread; its claims are given only as Moran presents them. These are two historians' objections, not the discipline's verdict; in period Prakash and Sarkar read her more favourably (edge_983).

proposed_edges.relationship: The co-editor of Selected Subaltern Studies (1988) questions Guha’s programme from within: his recovery of subaltern consciousness read as “a strategic use of positivist essentialism” (1985), and his insistence on the “full autonomy” of the subaltern domain not endorsed (1988)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: A repair to the pre-2000 core, from existing readings of her own texts. "Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography" (Subaltern Studies IV, 1985; read in full for revision 1.137): quoting Elementary Aspects while "Reading the work of Subaltern Studies from within but against the grain" (p. 341), she reads the project of retrieving subaltern consciousness "as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest" (p. 342). "Can the Subaltern Speak?" (1988; existing reading of the Williams and Chrisman reprint): of Guha's autonomous domain, "I cannot entirely endorse this insistence on determinate vigor and full autonomy" (p. 79). Collaboration in the same years: Selected Subaltern Studies (Oxford University Press, 1988), edited by Guha and Spivak (title as recorded on said_subaltern_foreword_1988; Roosa, 2006, n. 4, read). A later historian's summary: Eaton (2000, p. 60) reads the 1985 essay as criticism of "subalternist historians". edge_984 (Spivak → subaltern, critique) carries her critique of the collective's recovery of consciousness and its neglect of gender, and from this revision no longer names the autonomy claim in its relationship; this edge carries the person-to-person disagreement with Guha's autonomy claim, which Guha's own entry already names among the in-period critiques. A critique from a collaborator, not a rejection.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Would run parallel to edge_984 for the same pair; her later reformulations go into edge_984's note as an edge revision instead.
A programme for comparative literature; no historian's reading links it to global history.
Chibber has no node; their 2014 exchange is unread beyond opening lines and appears in the chronology and description, with Verso's quotations labelled.
Eagleton is in-period reception on edge_983 and edge_985; Chibber's argument against her is unread.
Kept with Eaton on the truthdebate arrow, since Moran cites Eaton and both answer the turn to literary reading of archives.

new_sources.title: Richard M. Eaton, "(Re)imag(in)ing Other²ness: A Postmortem for the Postmodern in India," Journal of World History 11:1 (2000): 57–78.
new_sources.citation: Richard M. Eaton, "(Re)imag(in)ing Other²ness: A Postmortem for the Postmodern in India," Journal of World History 11:1 (2000): 57–78.

verification.note: Read pp. 57–61 and 77–78 with notes 1–10; pp. 62–76 skimmed. Members of the collective shifted "from a positivist and empiricist orientation to one grounded more squarely in a literary criticism" (p. 60); "in the same volume [Subaltern Studies IV, 1985] Gayatri Spivak criticized subalternist historians for having adopted positivist methodologies"; "herself a literary critic, [she] urged historians to continue their efforts to recover subaltern consciousness even while knowing this was impossible" (p. 60, citing SS IV pp. 342, 345). His balance sheet: the turn's "modest reminder" is "vastly outweighed" by "a reinsertion of the British Raj to the center stage of Indian history, a neo-colonial vision of an essentialized India and Europe locked in implacable binary opposition, an ahistorical and structuralist methodology incapable of explaining historical particularity" (p. 78). His target is the postmodern turn in Indian history as a whole; Spivak and Cohn are named hinges.

verification.note: Read in part (abstract, introduction, the section on post-colonial discourse theory and Pahari sati, conclusion, notes 1–5; cited by section). Abstract: "a close reading of the records reveals profound discrepancies between Spivak's interpretation and conditions that existed in and around the kingdom at the time"; "the rani was actually an astute ruler, similar to her peers in the West Himalayan elite". Critique: "while Spivak concedes that her analysis is 'not historical work' insofar as 'historical knowledge cannot be established on single cases', her misreading of evidence goes beyond the boundaries of the discipline as such"; yet "her fresh approach to source material does point to the cardinal importance of interdisciplinary research". He cites Eaton (2000) in n. 3. His paraphrase of her 1988 answer as an unequivocal "no" is his reduction and is not reused.
